nodes.title: `gh issue create` errors after successful creation when issue type can't be set
nodes.body:
### Describe the bug

`gh issue create` shows an error message with "does not have the correct
permissions to execute `UpdateIssueIssueType`" - even though the issue was
created successfully. Occurs only when you dont have the right permissions on
the repo.

### Affected version

```bash
gh version 2.96.0 (2026-07-02)
```

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. gh issue create --repo <repo-with-issue-types> on a repo where you cant set the type
2. See the error

### Expected vs actual behavior

**Expected:** Issue created, no error message.

**Actual:** Issue created, then X operation failed... GraphQL: <user> does not
have the correct permissions to execute UpdateIssueIssueType.

### Logs

```bash
gh issue create --repo cli/cli

Creating issue in cli/cli

? Title (required) `gh issue create` errors after successful creation when issue type can't be set
? Choose a template 🐛 Bug report
? Body <Received>
? Issue type Bug
? What's next? Submit

nodes.title: [aw] Detection Runs
nodes.body:
This issue tracks all runs where threat detection flagged problems in agentic workflows in this repository. Each workflow run that completes with a detection warning or failure posts a comment here.

<details>
<summary>What is a Detection Problem?</summary>

A detection problem occurs when the threat detection system either:
- **Detects potential security threats** (prompt injection, secret leak, malicious patch)
- **Fails to produce results** (agent failure, parse error)

When `continue-on-error: true` (the default), these problems produce warnings and safe outputs still proceed. When `continue-on-error: false`, they block safe outputs entirely.

</details>

<details>
<summary>How This Helps</summary>

This issue helps you:
- Track workflows where threat detection raised concerns
- Review patterns of detection warnings or failures
- Identify false positives or recurring issues with threat detection
- Monitor the health of the threat detection system

</details>

<details>
<summary>Resources</summary>

- [GitHub Agentic Workflows Documentation](https://github.com/github/gh-aw)

</details>

> [!TIP]
> To configure threat detection behavior, update the frontmatter:
> ```yaml
> safe-outputs:
>   threat-detection:
>     continue-on-error: true   # Warnings only (default)
>     # continue-on-error: false  # Strict mode — block safe outputs
> ```

---

> This issue is automatically managed by GitHub Agentic Workflows. Do not close this issue manually.
>
> **No action to take** - Do not assign to an agent.

nodes.title: gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch: dependent PR closed instead of auto-retargeted to merged PR's base
nodes.body:
### What happened

A stacked-PR setup: PR #8 (`feat/fix` → base `feat/base`), where `feat/base`
was the head of open PR #7 (`feat/base` → `main`). The stack was assembled
with `gh stack init --adopt` — PR #7 predated the stack and was adopted as
the trunk when the descendant PR was created via `gh stack submit`. Both were
otherwise ordinary PRs with an ordinary base relationship.

I then ran: `gh pr merge 7 --squash --delete-branch`

Per the docs, deleting a merged PR's head branch should retarget open PRs
based on it to the merged PR's base branch. Instead, PR #8 was **closed**.

Timeline evidence (`gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/issues/8/timeline`):

- 19:56:28Z — PR #7 merged (squash)
- 19:56:29Z — `base_ref_deleted` event on PR #8
- 19:56:30Z — `closed` event on PR #8 (no retarget attempted)

### Recovery was a dead end

- `gh pr edit 8 --base main` on the closed PR: "Cannot change the base branch
  of a closed pull request."
- `gh pr reopen 8`: refused while the base branch was deleted (expected), but
  **also** refused after restoring the base branch, because the head branch
  had been rebased/pushed while the PR was closed. Catch-22: the PR had to be
  abandoned and recreated as a new PR, losing its identity.

### Questions

1. Is auto-retarget on branch deletion only wired to the web UI's post-merge
   "delete branch" flow, and not to a raw ref deletion via the REST API
   (which is what `--delete-branch` performs)?
2. If so, should `gh pr merge --delete-branch` warn when open PRs are based
   on the branch being deleted?

(If this is platform-side rather than CLI-side, happy to have it routed.)

nodes.title: Detect missing fine grain permission scopes, notify user on steps to take to refresh scopes

### Describe the bug

The Github REST API docs specify that creating a PR using a fine-grained permissions token only requires the 
> ["Pull requests" repository permissions (write)](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/pulls?apiVersion=2022-11-28#create-a-pull-request)

Adding this permission to the fine-grained token also automatically adds the "Metadata" permission as mandatory.

However, this results in an error along the lines of: `GraphQL: Resource not accessible by personal access token (repository.defaultBranchRef)`.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Create a fine-grained personal access token with the permissions:
    - Pull Requests: Read and write
    - Metadata (mandatory): Read-only
3. Locally, create a new branch in a repository, make a commit to it and push the branch to the remote
4. Run `gh pr create`, either interactively, or with flags
5. See an error like: `GraphQL: Resource not accessible by personal access token (repository.defaultBranchRef)`

If the "Contents: Read-only" permission is also added to the fine-grained personal access token, this issue goes away.

**Expected behaviour:** Able to create a PR using the GH CLI using a fine grained permissions token with permissions that are defined in the docs.
**Actual behaviour:** Extra permissions are required.

- An error in the docs
- REST API docs don't line up with the equivalent action(s) in the GH CLI

nodes.title: gh run view --job --log-failed fails on required shared-workflow metadata 404
nodes.body:
## Symptom

`gh run view RUN --job JOB --log-failed` fails before fetching logs for a completed organization-required workflow run:

```
failed to get run: HTTP 404: Not Found (https://api.github.com/repos/ORG/CONSUMER/actions/workflows/WORKFLOW_ID)
```

The same authenticated CLI can read the run metadata and download that job's logs directly. The workflow is required by an organization ruleset and originates in a shared workflow repository, rather than a workflow file in the consumer checkout.

## Repro

1. Configure a ruleset-required workflow from a shared repository and let its run complete for a consumer PR.
2. Obtain the run/job IDs from the PR check URL.
3. Run `gh run view RUN --repo ORG/CONSUMER --job JOB --log-failed`; it fails on the consumer repository's workflow metadata lookup above.
4. With the same authentication, `gh api repos/ORG/CONSUMER/actions/runs/RUN` succeeds, and `gh api --allow-escape-sequences repos/ORG/CONSUMER/actions/jobs/JOB/logs > job.log` succeeds. In the observed case the latter retrieved 81,118 bytes. Escape sequences were captured to a file, not printed to the terminal.

The run metadata's `workflow_id` is the ID in the failing URL, and `path` is `.github/workflows/review-gate.yml`. Repository/run IDs are redacted because this reproduction originated in application development.

## Expected

An explicit job-log request can read available job logs even when the optional workflow metadata lookup returns 404, or explains this workflow-source limitation without implying the run itself cannot be read.

## Environment

- `gh version 2.103.1 (2026-10-23)`
- macOS 27.0
- Observed 2026-10-26 while diagnosing a failed required review check.

I searched this tracker for required-workflow/run-view and workflow/not-found/log combinations before filing.

nodes.title: Add `gh run download` option to skip unpacking zip files
nodes.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

Sometimes, uploaded artifacts are folders containing a lot of files. This doesn't cause problems since the files are zipped automatically, and the zip can be downloaded from the Github website.
I would like the github CLI to have the feature to download the artifact zip *without extracting it*, for cases where you want to use it as a zip

### Proposed solution

Add a `--skip-unpack` flag to the command, which would write the zip file directly instead of extracting it

### Additional context

Here is such an usage of programmatic download of the zip file without unzipping it: https://github.com/WerWolv/ImHex/blob/6eedb469e97ba630f75e6e8c2a79b262e85f9043/.github/workflows/release.yml#L111

nodes.title: Windows: `gh extension upgrade`/`remove` delete the installed extension folder and leave it broken when a file in it is in use
nodes.body:
### Describe the bug

On Windows, `gh extension upgrade`, `gh extension remove` and `gh extension install` delete the installed extension's folder before doing anything else. If any file in it is in use, gh stops half-way and leaves an extension that `gh extension upgrade` can no longer repair.

The cause is in `pkg/cmd/extension/manager.go`. `installBin`, `installGit`, `InstallLocal` and `Remove` all call `cleanExtensionUpdateDir(name)` first:

```go
func (m *Manager) cleanExtensionUpdateDir(name string) error {
	if err := os.RemoveAll(m.UpdateDir(name)); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("failed to remove previous extension update state: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}
```

`UpdateDir(name)` is `config.StateDir()/extensions/<name>` and the install folder is `config.DataDir()/extensions/<name>`. On Linux and macOS these are different folders. On Windows, `go-gh/pkg/config` resolves both `StateDir()` and `DataDir()` to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GitHub CLI`, so the "update state" folder is the installed extension itself.

`os.RemoveAll` deletes what it can, including `manifest.yml`, and then fails on whatever is locked. Windows locks the extension's `.exe` while it runs, and it locks a folder that is any process's working directory. Without `manifest.yml` the extension is listed with no repo or version, and every later `gh extension upgrade` fails with `unable to retrieve latest version for extension "<name>"`. Only `remove` + `install` recovers.

This came in with #9934, which added the update-state folder. `github/gh-aw` ran into the same thing and traced it to the same lines (github/gh-aw#27269). They worked around it on their side, but this repo never got an issue.

### Affected version

```
gh version 2.102.0 (2026-09-30)
```

Also reproduced with 2.92.0 and 2.103.3. `cleanExtensionUpdateDir` is unchanged on `trunk`.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

On Windows, with any binary extension (`gh-foo` below):

1. `gh extension install owner/gh-foo`
2. Keep the extension running, e.g. a long-running `gh foo <command>` in one terminal. A terminal opened with `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GitHub CLI\extensions\gh-foo` as its working directory has the same effect.
3. In a second terminal: `gh extension remove foo`. `gh extension upgrade foo` takes the same path whenever an update is available.
4. `gh extension list`

### Expected vs actual behavior

Expected: gh only touches its own update state. An `upgrade` while the extension runs either succeeds (a running `.exe` can be renamed aside) or fails before changing the install, and the installed extension stays usable either way.

Actual (`upgrade` prints the same error after `[foo]: ` and then `some extensions failed to upgrade`):

```
failed to remove previous extension update state: unlinkat C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\GitHub CLI\extensions\gh-foo: The process cannot access the file because it is being used by another process.
```

`gh extension list` then shows `gh foo` with no repo and no version, `manifest.yml` is gone, and `gh extension upgrade foo` fails from then on with `unable to retrieve latest version` until `gh extension remove foo && gh extension install owner/gh-foo`.

Possible fixes, in increasing scope:
- Delete only the state file inside `UpdateDir(name)` instead of the folder, or skip `cleanExtensionUpdateDir` when `UpdateDir(name)` equals the install folder.
- Use a separate state folder on Windows, e.g. `%LOCALAPPDATA%\GitHub CLI\state`. Existing state would need a migration.

### Logs

The error above is the only output. The command is local file handling, so `GH_DEBUG=api` adds nothing past the release lookup.

nodes.title: `gh issue develop --base` outside a git repository creates the branch, then exits 1 without printing its URL
nodes.body:
### Describe the bug

`gh issue develop <n> -R OWNER/REPO --name <branch> --base <base>`, run from a directory that is not inside a git repository, creates the linked branch on GitHub, then exits 1 with `failed to run git: fatal: not in a git directory` and prints no URL. A branch that was created reads as a failed command, and a script that checks the exit code treats it as a failure. Repeating the command with the same `--name` outside a repository fails the same way, because the existing-branch path reaches the same step.

The cause is the order in `developRunCreate`: after `CreateLinkedBranch` succeeds ([develop.go#L261](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/674516ff39ccdaa8a525873f87552609dcda63de/pkg/cmd/issue/develop/develop.go#L261)), the `--base` value is written as `branch.<name>.gh-merge-base` with `git config` ([#L278-L283](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/674516ff39ccdaa8a525873f87552609dcda63de/pkg/cmd/issue/develop/develop.go#L278-L283)), and an error there returns before the URL is printed ([#L285](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/674516ff39ccdaa8a525873f87552609dcda63de/pkg/cmd/issue/develop/develop.go#L285)). The local steps after the URL already allow running outside a repository: `checkoutBranch` returns nil when no remotes are found, unless `--checkout` was given ([#L353-L364](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/674516ff39ccdaa8a525873f87552609dcda63de/pkg/cmd/issue/develop/develop.go#L353-L364)). The branch-config write is the one local step that assumes a repository. This code is the same on `trunk` (674516f) and in v2.103.3.

Related, not duplicates: the write came with the `gh-merge-base` support in #9712 (for #10089). #12575 and #12651 fixed a different failure of the same line (an empty branch name written into `.git/config`). #9072 asks in general for no repository requirement where an operation does not touch one; here the remote work succeeds and only the local base-branch hint fails.

### Affected version

```
gh version 2.96.0 (2026-07-02)
https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/tag/v2.96.0
```

Also reproduced with the latest release:

```
gh version 2.103.3 (2026-10-26)
https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/tag/v2.103.3
```

git version 2.50.1, Linux aarch64.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

Use a repository `OWNER/REPO` where you can create branches, an issue `<n>` in it with no linked branches, and an empty directory that is not inside a git repository. Times are UTC, 2026-10-28.

1. In the empty directory, gh 2.96.0, 14:47:24: `gh issue develop <n> -R OWNER/REPO --name <branch-a> --base main`. Exit 1, stdout empty, stderr `failed to run git: fatal: not in a git directory`. Afterwards `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/branches/<branch-a>` returns the branch and `gh issue develop --list <n> -R OWNER/REPO` lists it.
2. Control, same directory without `--base`, 14:47:26: `gh issue develop <n> -R OWNER/REPO --name <branch-b>`. Exit 0, prints `github.com/OWNER/REPO/tree/<branch-b>`.
3. Control, step 1's command in a fresh `git init` directory with no remotes, 14:47:28: `gh issue develop <n> -R OWNER/REPO --name <branch-c> --base main`. Exit 0, prints `github.com/OWNER/REPO/tree/<branch-c>`, and `git config --get branch.<branch-c>.gh-merge-base` there returns `main`.
4. Step 1 with gh 2.103.3, 14:47:44: `--name <branch-d>`. Exit 1, the same error, stdout empty, branch created.
5. Step 4 repeated with the same `--name <branch-d>`, 14:47:45. Exit 1, the same error; `GH_DEBUG=true` shows the failing call is `git config branch.<branch-d>.gh-merge-base main`.
6. Step 4 with a new name and `GH_DEBUG=true`, 14:47:53: `--name <branch-e>`. Exit 1, branch created; debug log below.

Before this reproduction the same failure showed up twice in normal use (2026-10-27 11:40Z and 2026-10-28 13:13Z), both run outside any repository, and in both GitHub's repository activity records the branch creation at the time of the failing call.

### Expected vs actual behavior

Expected: outside a repository, `--base` creates the branch, prints its URL and exits 0, as the command does without `--base`. The command's own code sets that behaviour for the other local steps: the test case "develop new branch outside of local git repo" in [develop_test.go](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/674516ff39ccdaa8a525873f87552609dcda63de/pkg/cmd/issue/develop/develop_test.go#L582) expects the URL and no error, and `checkoutBranch` bails out silently when "the command was not run from inside a git directory" ([#L356-L358](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/674516ff39ccdaa8a525873f87552609dcda63de/pkg/cmd/issue/develop/develop.go#L356-L358)). Inside a repository, `branch.<name>.gh-merge-base` is still written. With `--checkout`, an error outside a repository stays, as `checkoutBranch` already returns one.

Actual: exit 1, `failed to run git: fatal: not in a git directory`, no URL on stdout, and the linked branch exists on GitHub.

The existing outside-a-repository test case sets no `BaseBranch`, so this path has no test today; a `--base` variant of that case would cover it.

### Logs

```
# 2026-10-28T14:47:24Z, empty directory outside any git repository, gh 2.96.0
$ gh issue develop <n> -R OWNER/REPO --name <branch-a> --base main
failed to run git: fatal: not in a git directory
# exit 1, stdout empty

# 2026-10-28T14:47:26Z, same directory, no --base
$ gh issue develop <n> -R OWNER/REPO --name <branch-b>
github.com/OWNER/REPO/tree/<branch-b>
# exit 0

# 2026-10-28T14:47:28Z, fresh git init directory with no remotes
$ gh issue develop <n> -R OWNER/REPO --name <branch-c> --base main
github.com/OWNER/REPO/tree/<branch-c>
# exit 0
$ git config --get branch.<branch-c>.gh-merge-base
main

# 2026-10-28T14:47:35Z
$ gh issue develop --list <n> -R OWNER/REPO
<branch-a>	https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/tree/<branch-a>
<branch-b>	https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/tree/<branch-b>
<branch-c>	https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/tree/<branch-c>
```

<details><summary>GH_DEBUG=true, gh 2.103.3, step 6 (new branch, empty directory), full stderr, timestamps cut to milliseconds</summary>

```

nodes.title: `gh repo fork --remote` does not set a default repository, so `gh pr create` fails right after forking
nodes.body:
### Describe the bug

I had a clone of `mesonbuild/meson` with a single remote, `upstream`. To open a PR, I ran `gh repo fork --remote`, which added my fork as `origin`, and `git push` worked. Then `gh pr create` refused to run because no default repository was set.

Forking took me from one remote to two and left gh unable to pick one, even though the answer is obviously the repository I just forked. The `gh repo fork` help text even promises it: "The `upstream` remote will be set as the default remote repository." Only the `--clone` path does this, though. `--remote` in an existing clone never sets a default, whether the original remote was already named `upstream` or `origin` got renamed to `upstream`.

The same change was proposed in #12813, where a maintainer asked about the motivation behind it. I have a fix ready.

### Affected version

```
gh version 2.103.3 (2026-10-26)
https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/tag/v2.103.3
```

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. In a clone with a single remote pointing at someone else's repository, run `gh repo fork --remote`
2. Run `git push`
3. Run `gh pr create`

### Expected vs actual behavior

Expected: when no default is already set, `gh repo fork --remote` sets the remote for the forked repository as the default, just as `--clone` does.

Actual: no default is set, and `gh pr create` fails until I run `gh repo set-default` by hand.

### Logs

```
$ gh repo fork --remote
✓ Created fork HaraldNordgren/meson
✓ Added remote origin

$ gh pr create --web
X No default remote repository has been set. To learn more about the default repository, run: gh repo set-default --help
```

nodes.title: `--attach` cannot work for GitHub App installation tokens — the upload endpoint 404s them even with write access
nodes.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

The `--attach` stack (#14186) allowlists OAuth, classic PAT, and fine-grained PAT credentials, so a GitHub App installation token (`ghs_`) is rejected client-side with "unsupported authentication type".

We tested whether that allowlist is conservative or reflects the endpoint's actual behavior, since our automation runs on an installation token. Calling the endpoint directly from a GitHub Actions run (`GITHUB_TOKEN`, `permissions: contents: write`, private repo the token can push to):

```
POST https://uploads.github.com/user-attachments/assets?name=test.png&content_type=image/png&repository_id=<numeric id>
→ 404 {"message":"Not Found"}
```

The identical request with an OAuth token (`gho_`, same repo, WRITE permission) succeeds and returns an asset URL that renders in issues/PRs. So the exclusion is a property of the platform endpoint, not a CLI decision.

### Why it matters

Bots and CI are heavy producers of images on issues and PRs: verification screenshots, visual diffs, test artifacts. GitHub App tokens are the recommended identity for exactly that automation, yet they are the one credential class that cannot use the native attachment path. Our workaround today is committing images to a dedicated assets branch and embedding `raw/` URLs — the kind of hack `--attach` was built to retire.

### Proposed solution

1. If the token-type restriction is intentional platform behavior, say so here and route the ask upstream (github/roadmap#1324 makes no mention of credential-type requirements).
2. If the endpoint can be extended to installation tokens with write access, please allow them and widen `uploadTokenTypes` accordingly.
3. Either way, document the credential requirement in the `--attach` help, alongside the permission requirement requested in #14302.

nodes.title: `gh gist create` silently corrupts files that are not valid UTF-8
nodes.body:
### Describe the bug

`gh gist create` accepts files whose contents are not valid UTF-8, and uploads them with the invalid bytes silently replaced by U+FFFD. The gist is created, the command exits 0, and nothing warns that the contents that arrived are not the contents on disk.

Gist contents are sent as a JSON string. `encoding/json` does not reject invalid UTF-8, it rewrites every offending byte to U+FFFD, so anything that is not valid UTF-8 is quietly mangled in transit.

The binary check that is supposed to catch this classifies contents by MIME type:

```go
// pkg/cmd/gist/shared/shared.go
func IsBinaryContents(contents []byte) bool {
	isBinary := true
	for mime := mimetype.Detect(contents); mime != nil; mime = mime.Parent() {
		if mime.Is("text/plain") {
			isBinary = false
			break
		}
	}
	return isBinary
}
```

MIME sniffing and "survives a JSON round trip" are not the same question, so this misses text-like encodings. latin-1 and UTF-16 both sniff as `text/plain`, pass the check, and are then corrupted by the encoder.

### Affected version

```
gh version 2.98.0
https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/tag/v2.98.0
```

Also present on `trunk` at a255baf7.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Create a file that is text, but not UTF-8. Any file saved as ISO-8859-1 with an accented character will do:

   ```sh
   printf 'caf\xe9 r\xe9sum\xe9\n' > latin1.txt
   ```

2. Create a gist from it:

   ```sh
   gh gist create latin1.txt
   ```

3. The command succeeds and prints a gist URL.

4. Read the file back and compare it to the original:

   ```sh
   gh gist view <gist-id> --raw | xxd | head
   xxd latin1.txt | head
   ```

### Expected vs actual behavior

**Expected:** either the file is uploaded unchanged, or `gh` refuses it and says why. Silently changing the contents is the one outcome that should not happen.

**Actual:** each `0xe9` byte is replaced by `0xef 0xbf 0xbd` (U+FFFD, the replacement character). The 12-byte file above is stored as 18 bytes:

```
sent on the wire: {"files":{"latin1.txt":{"content":"caf� r�sum�\n"}}}

on disk:  63 61 66 e9 20 72 e9 73 75 6d e9 0a            "café résumé\n"
in gist:  63 61 66 ef bf bd 20 72 ef bf bd 73 75 6d ef bf bd 0a
```

The original bytes are not recoverable from the gist afterwards.

### Notes

There is a second, opposite symptom of the same check, already reported as #9761: most ASCII control characters sniff as binary, so a plain text file containing one is rejected with `binary file not supported` even though the API accepts it and the same gist can be created in the browser.

So the current check is wrong in both directions — it rejects contents the API handles fine, and accepts contents it cannot carry losslessly. Checking `utf8.Valid` instead answers the question that actually matters, and lines up exactly with what survives the round trip.

Incidentally, the existing test fixture for "binary" contents in `pkg/cmd/gist/shared/shared_test.go` is a run of `239, 191, 189` bytes — that is U+FFFD repeated, so the JPEG it was taken from had already been through this same lossy conversion before it was captured as test data.

I have a fix for both directions and am happy to open a PR.

nodes.title: Expiring token auto-refresh can break the stored login when `gh` runs in a sandbox without write access
nodes.body:
### Describe the bug

When signed in with an expiring token (`gh auth login --expiring`), `gh` refreshes the access token automatically and proactively, whenever any command runs within 10 minutes of expiry. Each refresh rotates the refresh token: the server issues a new one and invalidates the old one. To do this safely, `gh` relies on write access to three places: a lock file (`refresh.lock`) in its state directory that makes parallel `gh` processes refresh only once, the system keyring where the credential is stored by default, and its config directory (`hosts.yml`, which also holds the credential when plaintext storage is used).

Sandboxed environments, such as the default sandboxes of coding agents, often allow network access while making the user's home directory and keyring read only. In that setup:

1. Taking the lock is best effort, so when the state directory is read only `gh` proceeds without it. Parallel `gh` processes, which are common with agents, can then all try to refresh with the same refresh token. Only the first succeeds and the rest are rejected.
2. The successful refresh rotates the refresh token on the server, but saving the new credential to the keyring or config fails, so `gh` keeps the old credential that the server has just invalidated.
3. Every later `gh` invocation, inside or outside the sandbox, presents the invalidated refresh token and fails, and the user has to run `gh auth login` again.

### Affected version

```
gh version 2.103.2 (2026-10-23)
https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/tag/v2.103.2
```

All versions since v2.103.0 are affected when using an expiring token.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. Sign in with `gh auth login --expiring` using keyring storage.
2. Start a sandbox that allows network access but makes `~/.config/gh`, `~/.local/state/gh`, and the keyring read only (for example, a coding agent's default workspace sandbox with network access enabled).
3. When the access token is within 10 minutes of expiry, run any `gh` command that calls the API inside the sandbox, ideally several in parallel.
4. Outside the sandbox, run `gh auth status`.

### Expected vs actual behavior

Expected: `gh` either refreshes and saves the new credential, or, when it cannot save it, does not refresh and leaves the stored login usable (using the current access token while it is still valid, or failing with a clear message explaining why refresh is not possible).

Actual: the refresh rotates the token on the server without saving the result, and the stored login becomes unusable everywhere until the user signs in again.

### Logs

N/A

nodes.title: `auth refresh` makes it easy to authorise the wrong account in the browser
nodes.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

Currently, `gh auth refresh` only refreshes the active account. The [help text](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/93d24ce9ffefb6cc86bde89b50271457bb0ef9cb/pkg/cmd/auth/refresh/refresh.go#L79-L81) says that to refresh another account you have to `gh auth switch` to it first, and then switch back when you are done.

That part is fine, but the browser has no idea which account `gh` is refreshing. When I am signed in to multiple accounts on github.com, the device flow page shows a multi account interstitial asking which account to continue with. Nothing on that page tells me which account `gh` expects, so it is easy to pick the wrong one.

If I do, I only find out at the very end, when `gh` rejects the token [here](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/93d24ce9ffefb6cc86bde89b50271457bb0ef9cb/pkg/cmd/auth/refresh/refresh.go#L279-L282):

```go
return fmt.Errorf("error refreshing credentials for %s, received credentials for %s, did you use the correct account in the browser?", activeUser, result.Username)
```

At that point the device code has been used, so the only option is to run the whole flow again and hope I click the right account this time.

### Proposed solution

I don't think `gh` can fix this on its own, because the account picker lives on the OAuth page. OpenID Connect defines a [`login_hint`](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#AuthRequest) parameter for exactly this, so the client can tell the server which account it expects.

### Acceptance Criteria

**Given** I am signed in to github.com in my browser as `monalisa` and `hubot`
**And Given** `monalisa` is the active account in `gh auth status`
**When** I run `gh auth refresh` and open the verification URL
**Then** the browser only offers to continue as `monalisa`

nodes.title: Upcoming PGP signing key rotation for GitHub CLI Linux packages [September 2026]
nodes.body: > [!NOTE] > This issue only affects Linux users who install `gh` from our APT or RPM package repositories. If you are on Windows or macOS, or you installed `gh` via Homebrew, GitHub Releases, or built from source code, this does not apply to you. - [What's happening?](#whats-happening) - [Am I affected?](#am-i-affected) - [How to confirm locally installed keyring?](#how-to-confirm-locally-installed-keyring) - [Debian/Ubuntu](#debianubuntu) - [RHEL/Fedora/CentOS/openSUSE/SUSE/Amazon Linux 2](#rhelfedoracentosopensusesuseamazon-linux-2) - [What do I need to do?](#what-do-i-need-to-do) - [New users](#new-users) - [Existing APT users (Debian/Ubuntu)](#existing-apt-users-debianubuntu) - [Docker build failing?](#docker-build-failing) - [Existing RPM users (Fedora, RHEL, CentOS, Amazon Linux 2, openSUSE/SUSE)](#existing-rpm-users-fedora-rhel-centos-amazon-linux-2-opensusesuse) - [DNF5 (Fedora 41 or newer)](#dnf5-fedora-41-or-newer) - [DNF4 (CentOS, RHEL, Fedora 40 or earlier)](#dnf4-centos-rhel-fedora-40-or-earlier) - [Yum (Amazon Linux 2)](#yum-amazon-linux-2) - [Zypper (openSUSE/SUSE)](#zypper-opensusesuse) - [Removing old key from RPM keyrings](#removing-old-key-from-rpm-keyrings) - [Background](#background) - [Final notes](#final-notes) ## What's happening? The PGP key currently used to verify GitHub CLI Linux packages is expiring on **Saturday, September 5, 2026**. We have generated a new key and have already published an updated keyring file that contains both the old and new keys on **Wednesday, April 8, 2026**. This table lists the current and the new PGP key fingerprint: | Key | Fingerprint | |---|---| | Current key (expires September 5, 2026) | `2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059` | | New key | `7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325` | > [!NOTE] > The new key does not have a fixed expiration date, but this does not necessarily mean that it is permanent. Choosing a key without a fixed expiration date supports our goal of keeping package installation and update processes smooth while minimizing disruption to our users. If and when we decide to rotate this key, we will announce the change publicly and provide clear instructions for any required action. As a background, back in September 2024, [our PGP signing key expired (#9569)](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/9569), disrupting Linux package installs and updates. At that time, we extended the expiration of the existing key as an emergency fix. This time, however, we are proactively rotating to a brand-new key well ahead of the expiry date. Check out [Am I affected?](#am-i-affected) below to see if you are going to be affected by this change. For affected users, package install and update operations that rely on the old key will start failing after the expiry date unless you follow the steps outlined in this document. Typical error/warning messages look like any of the following: ``` W: Failed to fetch https://cli.github.com/packages/dists/stable/InRelease The following signatures were invalid: EXPKEYSIG 23F3D4EA75716059 GitHub CLI The following signatures couldn't be verified because the public key is not available: NO_PUBKEY 5612B36462313325 ``` ``` Transaction failed: Signature verification failed. OpenPGP check for package ... from repo "gh-cli" has failed: Import of the key didn't help, wrong key? ``` ``` The GPG keys listed for the "packages for the GitHub CLI" repository are already installed but they are not correct for this package. Check that the correct key URLs are configured for this repository.. Failing package is: gh... GPG Keys are configured as: https://keyserver.ubuntu.com/pks/lookup?op=get&search=0x23F3D4EA75716059 ... Error: GPG check FAILED ``` ``` The GPG keys listed for the "packages for the GitHub CLI" repository are already installed but they are not correct for this package. Check that the correct key URLs are configured for this repository. Failing package is: gh... GPG Keys are configured as: https://keyserver.ubuntu.com/pks/lookup?op=get&search=0x23F3D4EA75716059 ``` ``` Warning: File 'repomd.xml' from repository 'packages for the GitHub CLI' is signed with an unknown key '5612B36462313325' ... Warning: We can't verify that no one meddled with this file, so it might not be trustworthy anymore! You should not continue unless you know it's safe. ... Repository 'packages for the GitHub CLI' is invalid. [gh-cli|https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm] Valid metadata not found at specified URL History: - Signature verification failed for repomd.xml - Can't provide /repodata/repomd.xml ``` ``` gh-... (packages for the GitHub CLI): Signature verification failed [4-Signatures public key is not available] ``` ``` Warning: File 'repomd.xml' from repository 'packages for the GitHub CLI' is signed with an unknown key '5612B36462313325' ... Warning: We can't verify that no one meddled with this file, so it might not be trustworthy anymore! You should not continue unless you know it's safe. ... Repository 'packages for the GitHub CLI' is invalid. [gh-cli|https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm] Failed to retrieve new repository metadata. History: - Signature verification failed for repomd.xml ``` ``` error: Verifying a signature using certificate 2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059 (GitHub CLI ): 1. Certificate 23F3D4EA75716059 invalid: certificate is not alive because: The primary key is not live because: Expired on 2026-09-05T12:44:10Z 2. Key 23F3D4EA75716059 invalid: key is not alive because: The primary key is not live because: Expired on 2026-09-05T12:44:10Z ``` ## Am I affected? | Scenario | Affected? | |---|---| | You cannot install or upgrade `gh` | Probably. See [Existing APT users](#existing-apt-users-debianubuntu) or [Existing RPM users](#existing-rpm-users-fedora-rhel-centos-amazon-linux-2-opensusesuse). | | Installed `gh` via `apt` **before** the new keyring was published (April 8, 2026) and haven't re-run the installation steps since | **Yes**. See [Existing APT users](#existing-apt-users-debianubuntu). | | Installed `gh` via `dnf`, `yum`, or `zypper` **before** the new keyring was published (April 8, 2026) and haven't re-run the installation steps since | **Yes**. See [Existing RPM users](#existing-rpm-users-fedora-rhel-centos-amazon-linux-2-opensusesuse). | | Installed `gh` using official docs **after** the new keyring was published (April 8, 2026) | **No**. Your keyring already contains the new key. | | Installed `gh` via Homebrew, Conda, a community package manager, or from precompiled binaries | **No**. These methods do not use our PGP key. | | You do not remember when you installed `gh` | See [How to confirm locally installed keyring?](#how-to-confirm-locally-installed-keyring) | ## How to confirm locally installed keyring? If you do not remember when you installed `gh` from the official docs, you can easily confirm if you are going to be affected by checking your local configuration. Follow the subsection that applies to you. ### Debian/Ubuntu > [!TIP] > If `gpg` is not installed, you can install it with: > ```shell > sudo apt update > sudo apt install gnupg > ``` Check how many keys are in your local keyring file: ```shell gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg ``` > [!TIP] > If the file is not found at that path, try the older location: > > ```shell > gpg --show-keys /usr/share/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg > ``` > > If you still cannot find the keyring file, check your APT source entry to see the path it references: > > ```shell > cat /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list > ``` > > Look for the `signed-by=` value in the output, which points to your keyring file path. If the output shows **two** public key entries (with fingerprints `2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059` and `7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325`), you already have the updated keyring and no action is needed. This is what the output should look like: ``` pub rsa4096 2022-09-06 [SC] [expires: 2026-09-05] 2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059 uid GitHub CLI sub rsa4096 2022-09-06 [E] [expires: 2026-09-05] pub rsa4096 2026-04-07 [SC] 7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325 uid GitHub CLI sub rsa4096 2026-04-07 [E] ``` If only **one** key is listed (the old key `2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059`), you need to update your keyring. See [Existing APT users](#existing-apt-users-debianubuntu). ### RHEL/Fedora/CentOS/openSUSE/SUSE/Amazon Linux 2 Check which GitHub CLI keys are imported in your RPM keyring: ```shell rpm -qa gpg-pubkey | xargs -I{} sh -c 'rpm -qi {} | grep -q "opensource+cli@github.com" && echo {}' ``` If the output includes **only** one entry (the old key), you will need to update. See [Existing RPM users](#existing-rpm-users-fedora-rhel-centos-amazon-linux-2-opensusesuse). If you see a second key entry, your system already has the new key and no action is needed. ## What do I need to do? ### New users If you are installing `gh` for the first time, simply follow the standard [Linux installation instructions](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/docs/install_linux.md). The current keyring file already contains the new key, so no extra steps are needed. This also applies if you installed `gh` for the first time after the new keyring was published (April 8, 2026). ### Existing APT users (Debian/Ubuntu) You need to replace your local copy of the keyring file. Run either of the following commands to download the updated keyring: ```shell # Using wget sudo mkdir -p -m 755 /etc/apt/keyrings sudo wget -qO /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg \ && sudo chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg # Using curl sudo mkdir -p -m 755 /etc/apt/keyrings sudo curl -fsSL -o /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg \ && sudo chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg ``` Then update your package lists and upgrade `gh`: ```shell sudo apt update sudo apt install gh ``` > [!NOTE] > If your keyring file is located elsewhere (e.g., under `/usr/share/keyrings/`), you should update that path in the command above. However, the recommended location is `/etc/apt/keyrings/`. Regardless of the path, make sure the `signed-by` field in the APT source entry (at `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list`) points at the right keyring file. > [!TIP] > You can verify the updated keyring contains both keys by running: > ```shell > gpg --show-keys /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg > ``` > You should see an output like this: > ``` > pub rsa4096 2022-09-06 [SC] [expired: 2026-09-05] > 2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059 > uid GitHub CLI > sub rsa4096 2022-09-06 [E] [expired: 2026-09-05] > > pub rsa4096 2026-04-07 [SC] > 7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325 > uid GitHub CLI > sub rsa4096 2026-04-07 [E] > ``` #### Docker build failing? If your Docker build is failing because a layer previously added our package repository and a later layer runs `apt update` or `apt-get update`, you need to ensure the updated keyring is present. If you control the layer that adds the keyring, rebuild it so it pulls the latest keyring file. If you don't control that layer, add a new layer **before** any `apt update` or `apt-get update` that fetches the updated keyring: ```dockerfile RUN wget -qO /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg \ && chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg ``` Or if you prefer using `curl`: ```dockerfile RUN curl -fsSL -o /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg \ && chmod go+r /etc/apt/keyrings/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg ``` If you don't use `gh` at all and it just happens to be in a base image, you can remove the repository so that `apt update` or `apt-get update` no longer try to verify it: ```shell sudo rm /etc/apt/sources.list.d/github-cli.list ``` ### Existing RPM users (Fedora, RHEL, CentOS, Amazon Linux 2, openSUSE/SUSE) RPM-based systems import PGP keys into their own keyring at install time. To pick up the new key, you need to re-fetch the repository configuration file, which now references an updated keyring. Choose the instructions matching your package manager below. Note that when upgrading `gh` at the end, your package manager will prompt you to confirm importing the PGP keys. Verify that the key fingerprints match the following: - Old key: `2C6106201985B60E6C7AC87323F3D4EA75716059` - New key: `7F38BBB59D064DBCB3D84D725612B36462313325` > [!IMPORTANT] > Instructions below mimic our [Linux installation guide](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/docs/install_linux.md). So, please make sure you follow the heading that you originally used to install `gh`. #### DNF5 (Fedora 41 or newer) > [!TIP] > Run `dnf --version` if you are unsure what version you are using. > [!NOTE] > Ensure the `config-manager` plugin is installed (for example, `sudo dnf install dnf5-plugins`). ```shell sudo dnf config-manager addrepo --overwrite --from-repofile=https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo sudo dnf update gh ``` #### DNF4 (CentOS, RHEL, Fedora 40 or earlier) > [!TIP] > Run `dnf --version` if you are unsure what version you are using. > [!NOTE] > Ensure the `config-manager` plugin is installed (for example, `sudo dnf install 'dnf-command(config-manager)'`). ```shell sudo dnf config-manager --add-repo https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo sudo dnf update gh ``` #### Yum (Amazon Linux 2) > [!NOTE] > Ensure the `config-manager` plugin is installed (for example, `sudo yum install yum-utils`). ```shell sudo yum-config-manager --add-repo https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo sudo yum update gh ``` #### Zypper (openSUSE/SUSE) ```shell sudo zypper removerepo gh-cli sudo zypper addrepo https://cli.github.com/packages/rpm/gh-cli.repo sudo zypper update gh ``` #### Removing old key from RPM keyrings If you still encounter key verification errors after re-adding the repository, you may need to remove the old key from the RPM keyring first: 1. Find the old PGP key: ```shell sudo rpm -qa gpg-pubkey ``` Our old PGP key is usually named `gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a` or `gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a`. You can confirm the correct key by checking its Packager field: ```shell sudo rpm -qi gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a # or sudo rpm -qi gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a ``` The Packager should be `GitHub CLI `. 2. Once you have confirmed the Packager, remove the old PGP key: ```shell sudo rpm -e gpg-pubkey-75716059-63172e8a # or sudo rpm -e gpg-pubkey-2c6106201985b60e6c7ac87323f3d4ea75716059-63172e8a ``` 3. Then remove and reinstall `gh`: ```shell sudo dnf remove gh sudo dnf install gh ``` (Replace `dnf` with `yum` or `zypper` as appropriate.) ## Background In September 2024, [our PGP signing key expired (#9569)](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/9569), disrupting Linux package installs and updates. At that time, we extended the expiration of the existing key as an emergency fix. This time, we are proactively rotating to a brand-new key well ahead of the expiry date. The updated keyring files (binary [`.gpg`](https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.gpg) and ASCII armored [`.asc`](https://cli.github.com/packages/githubcli-archive-keyring.asc)) already contain both the old and new keys, so anyone who has installed `gh` following our [Linux installation instructions](https://github.com/cli/cli/blob/trunk/docs/install_linux.md) since April 8, 2026, is already covered. ## Final notes We apologize for any inconvenience this may cause. By announcing well in advance, we hope to give everyone enough time to update their keyring before the old key expires. If you run into any problems, please follow up on this issue and we'll do our best to help. Thank you for your patience and for using GitHub CLI!

nodes.title: gh skill install --all: identical skills under skills/ and plugins/<name>/skills/ are rejected as conflicting names
nodes.body:
### Describe the bug

A repository that ships its Agent Skills both at the root (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, the Agent Skills convention) and inside a Claude Code / Cursor plugin folder (`plugins/<plugin>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, a byte-identical copy the plugin needs to be self-contained) cannot be installed with `--all`: discovery finds both and refuses.

### Steps to reproduce

```
gh skill install ChanMeng666/archlang --all --agent cursor --scope project
```

```
Note: found 5 skill(s) using the plugins/ convention
cannot install skills with conflicting names; they would overwrite each other:
  archlang: [plugins] archlang/archlang, archlang
  archlang-export: [plugins] archlang/archlang-export, archlang-export
  ...
```

Installing by path (`gh skill install ChanMeng666/archlang skills/archlang`) works.

### Expected behavior

When two discovered skills share a name and their contents are identical, install one of them (or prefer the root `skills/` copy over the `plugins/` one) instead of failing. Shipping the same skills as a standalone set and as part of a plugin is common, since plugin folders must be self-contained.

### Environment

gh version 2.96.0 (2026-07-02), Windows 11.

nodes.title: gh extension upgrade should support upgrading to the "latest" prerelease (as well as supporting `--pin`)
nodes.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you’d like to solve

`gh extension upgrade` should allow flexibility when dealing with prerelease extensions, both by allowing an upgrade directly to the latest prerelease, and by supporting a `--pin` flag.

Currently:

```shellsession
$ gh extension upgrade ext
[ext]: already up to date
✓ Successfully checked extension upgrades

$ gh extension upgrade ext --pin v1.0.0.beta.2
unknown flag: --pin

Usage:  gh extension upgrade {<name> | --all} [flags]

Flags:
  --all       Upgrade all extensions
  --dry-run   Only display upgrades
  --force     Force upgrade extension
```

### Proposed solution

* add a `--latest-prerelease` flag that lets the version be drawn from prereleases as well, sorting by version order
* add a `--to <ver>` flag that will accept any version, prerelease or otherwise

That'll mean that we don't need to fully release an extension to GA in order to test it.

### Additional context

Add any other context like screenshots or mockups are helpful, if applicable.

nodes.title: gh variable/secret commands should url-encode environment name
nodes.body:
### Describe the bug

Environment name is not escaped in the `gh secret` and `gh variable` commands, so the API request fails.

```
$ gh --version
gh version 2.45.0 (2024-03-04)
https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/tag/v2.45.0
```

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

When referring to an environment with `/` symbol in the name, request fails because it breaks the endpoint URL:

```
$ gh variable list --env 'foo/buh'
failed to get variables: HTTP 404: Not Found (https://api.github.com/repos/laughedelic/test-repo/environments/foo/buh/variables?per_page=100)
```


### Expected vs actual behavior

Expected: `gh variable list --env 'foo/buh'` should work and make a request to

```
https://api.github.com/repos/laughedelic/test-repo/environments/foo%2Fbuh/variables?per_page=100
```

i.e. URL-encoding the environment name. Instead it makes a request to 

```
https://api.github.com/repos/laughedelic/test-repo/environments/foo/buh/variables?per_page=100
```

URL-encoding the environment name manually works, for example using jq:

```
$ gh variable list --env $(jq -rn --arg env 'foo/buh' '$env|@uri')
NAME                   VALUE                     UPDATED
VARIABLE_NAME          some_value                about 20 days ago
```

---

I don't know if this applies to more commands, but it definitely does for both `gh variable` and `gh secret`

nodes.title: gh auth status should distinguish transport failures from invalid credentials
nodes.body:
## Summary
`gh auth status` currently reports that a token is invalid when the underlying failure is actually at the network/transport layer. In restricted environments this sends users toward re-authentication even though their credentials may be fine.

## Example Use Case
A concrete case is running `gh auth status` inside a sandboxed or otherwise restricted environment where DNS or outbound network access is blocked. In that situation the human-readable output says the token is invalid, but the actual failure is a transport error such as `lookup api.github.com: no such host`. Running the same command outside the restricted environment succeeds without re-authentication.

This can also apply in CI, containers, devboxes, or corporate network setups where GitHub is temporarily unreachable or DNS/proxy configuration is broken.

## Reproduction
1. Run `gh auth status` in an environment with blocked DNS or blocked outbound access to GitHub.
2. Observe that the human-readable output says the token is invalid and suggests `gh auth login` or `gh auth logout`.
3. Run `gh auth status --json hosts` or `GH_DEBUG=api gh auth status`.
4. Observe that the real error is transport-related, for example `lookup api.github.com: no such host`.
5. Run the same command outside the restricted environment and see authentication succeed.

## Current Behavior
- Human-readable output reports an authentication problem.
- Machine-readable/debug output can already show the real transport error.

## Expected Behavior
- Human-readable output should distinguish invalid credentials from transport/network verification failures.
- Re-authentication guidance should only be shown for actual invalid-credential failures.
- If maintainers prefer a minimal change, JSON output can remain backward compatible while the human-readable messaging is corrected.

## Additional Context
I already implemented a draft fix in PR #12878, which keeps the JSON shape stable and only changes the human-readable classification/message path.

nodes.title: [aw] No-Op Runs
nodes.body:
This issue tracks all no-op runs from agentic workflows in this repository. Each workflow run that completes with a no-op message (indicating no action was needed) posts a comment here.

<details>
<summary>What is a No-Op?</summary>

A no-op (no operation) occurs when an agentic workflow runs successfully but determines that no action is required. For example:
- A security scanner that finds no issues
- An update checker that finds nothing to update
- A monitoring workflow that finds everything is healthy

These are successful outcomes, not failures, and help provide transparency into workflow behavior.

</details>

<details>
<summary>How This Helps</summary>

This issue helps you:
- Track workflows that ran but determined no action was needed
- Distinguish between failures and intentional no-ops
- Monitor workflow health by seeing when workflows decide not to act

</details>

<details>
<summary>Resources</summary>

- [GitHub Agentic Workflows Documentation](https://github.com/github/gh-aw)

</details>

> [!TIP]
> To stop a workflow from posting here, set `report-as-issue: false` in its frontmatter:
> ```yaml
> safe-outputs:
>   noop:
>     report-as-issue: false
> ```

---

> This issue is automatically managed by GitHub Agentic Workflows. Do not close this issue manually.
> 
> **No action to take** - Do not assign to an agent.

### Proposed solution

first does
